In this article GOOGL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Google has been ordered to halt work on two data centers it's developing in Finland, a month after the tech giant committed to investing $15 billion in AI infrastructure in the country. Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency (LVV) on Tuesday issued a notice to Google subsidiary, Tuike Finland Oy, to suspend building work for data center projects planned for Muhos and Kajaani until the environmental impact assessments have been completed. The suspension request applies, among other things, to the removal of trees, removal of topsoil, excavation, quarrying, crushing, transfer of soil masses, ditching and the construction of roads and storage areas, according to a Google translation of an LVV press release. "We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance," a Google spokesperson told CNBC, adding that they would follow the LVV's guidance. "We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas," the spokesperson said. "As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos." watch now VIDEO 6:02 06:02 Fortum CEO on Google’s €13 bln Finland push Squawk Box Europe The LVV ordered Google to halt work no later than Oct. 23. The request does not apply to planning, measurements, soil surveys, or other measures with minor impacts that can be easily restored. "In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure," Tommi Muilu, head of the environmental department at the Finnish licensing and supervision authority, said in the statement. 'Texas of Europe' Finland has emerged as a key location for data centers amid the AI boom, with hyperscalers and developers eyeing its available land and power, which is in short supply throughout most of Europe. Several data center projects with potential capacities of hundreds of megawatts have recently been announced in the country. The rise in demand has led to Finland being dubbed the "Texas of Europe." The U.S. state has become one of the leading locations for AI data centers globally, with a number of huge projects announced by hyperscalers and AI labs , including Google, Meta , Microsoft and Anthropic. Google's $15 billion plan for Finland will mark its largest investment in Europe. The capital will be deployed through 2028 into data centers and other supporting investments like energy projects, the company said in a statement at the time. Noam Galai | Getty Images Entertainment | Getty Images Luxury carmaker Jaguar has launched its new all-electric vehicle, two years after the famed British company's controversial rebrand prompted a social media backlash. The automotive manufacturer, which is owned by India's Tata Motors , unveiled the Type 01 model on Tuesday at an event in New York City, describing it as the "most technically advanced" and "most powerful and aerodynamic" Jaguar ever. It marks a radical new direction for the company, which was criticized in November 2024 when it revealed a series of changes ahead of becoming a fully electric brand. Jaguar posted a 30-second clip on X at the time which featured several models in brightly colored clothing and marketing slogans such as "live vivid", "delete ordinary" and "copy nothing." Notably, the ad did not feature a car or the company's traditional cat logo. Among those to criticize the ad was Elon Musk , with the owner of the X social media platform asking : "Do you sell cars?" Jaguar sought to defend the ad campaign, telling Sky News at the time that the company wanted "to be bold and disruptive." Italy's Ferrari and Britain's Bentley have also launched their first EV models this year, seeking to test wealthy buyers' appetite for going electric as luxury carmakers seek to compete with cheaper Chinese car brands. Jaguar's Type 01 has a starting price of £130,000 (roughly $172,000) in the U.K. and around $130,500 in the U.S., according to multiple media reports , which is significantly higher than previous comparable models. Jaguar later confirmed to CNBC on Wednesday morning that the Type 01 model has a minimum price tag of $130,000 in North America. The four-door "Grand Tourer" has an ultra-long bonnet, low roofline, frameless doors and a camera instead of a rear window. It has a range of up to 450 miles and can accelerate from 0-62 miles per hour in 3.2 seconds. Rawdon Glover speaks during the Jaguar Type 01 Launch Event at Storied NYC on October 06, 2026 in New York City. Noam Galai | Getty Images Entertainment | Getty Images The launch of the model comes as Jaguar Land Rover continues its recovery from a cyberattack that forced the company to halt production last year, and one month after JLR announced it would cut 4,000 jobs as part of a major cost-cutting drive. JLR CEO PB Balaji described the unveiling of Type 01 as the start of "an exciting new era" for Jaguar. "Combining British heritage, bold creativity, advanced technology and groundbreaking engineering, it reflects our ambition to create objects of desire that will help us invite a new generation of clients into Jaguar's loyal and passionate customer base," Balaji said in a statement. headlines.title: Chevron CEO warns against 'unwise' diesel export ban, saying it could make things worse
headlines.summary: His comments come as rising Middle East crude exports and an emergency G7 stockpile release appear to have helped to ease supply fears.
headlines.article_text: Chevron CEO warns against 'unwise' diesel export ban Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC that a U.S. diesel export ban would be “unwise,” saying it could worsen supply pressures and undermine confidence in the U.S. as a reliable energy supplier. Global supply fears have eased following higher Middle East crude exports and a G7 emergency stockpile release, but markets remain on edge as the U.S.-Iran war drags on. In this article CVX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:20 06:20 Chevron CEO says low reserves leave energy system vulnerable to disruption Squawk Box Europe The chief executive of U.S. oil giant Chevron on Wednesday warned that it would be "unwise" for the Trump administration to move forward with a diesel export ban , saying the policy risks worsening the supply situation. "Export bans, be they in the U.S. or in other countries, actually take supply off the global market and they run the risk of making the situation worse," Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC's " Squawk Box Europe " in an exclusive interview on Wednesday. "The U.S. has been a reliable supplier to the world at a time when it needs it," he continued. "And I think it would be unwise for the U.S. to create questions in the minds of our allies and our partners as to whether or not we will be there with reliable supply when times are difficult — and so, there are other options." His comments come as rising Middle East crude exports and an emergency G7 stockpile release appear to have helped to ease supply fears, although energy market participants remain on edge as Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthi forces exchange attacks . The U.S.-Iran war has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway that typically handles around 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, sending shock waves through the global economy. A sign displays the prices of unleaded gasoline and diesel fuel at a Chevron gas station in Bay Harbor Island, Florida, US, on Monday, June 22, 2026. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty Images U.S. President Donald Trump , who has cooled on the prospect of authorizing a diesel export ban after G7 countries agreed to release diesel and crude oil from their emergency reserves, recently allowed the use of cheaper red-dyed diesel to be used more broadly in part of a push to bring down record-high fuel costs. Trump signed an executive order Monday evening stateside to temporarily allow truckers and farmers to use red-dyed diesel — which is exempt from highway fuel taxes — and deferred related taxes on the fuel through the end of this year. The tax-free diesel is typically used by farm equipment, construction machinery, trucks and other off-road vehicles. It is therefore exempt from a 24.4-cent-per-gallon tax applied to diesel fuel sold for highway transportation. Energy system 'more vulnerable to disruption' Asked how fragile the global inventory position is ahead of winter, Chevron's CEO described it as a "very serious" situation. "We came into this year with high inventories. High inventories in commercial stocks held by companies, high inventories in strategic stocks held by governments around the world and actually significant inventories on the water, particularly barrels that were sanctioned by the U.S. or the EU," Wirth said. "Over the last several months, we've seen commercial inventories draw down, strategic stocks be released and those sanctioned barrels have been relieved and allowed to be delivered as well," he continued. "Those are all buffers in the system that have bought us time, but they've been drained. And so, we're at much lower levels of inventory right now and it makes the system more vulnerable to disruption." Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said earlier this week that it could take up to two years to rebuild global oil inventories, warning that the squeeze on supplies could yet get worse as the U.S.-Iran war drags on. Venezuela outlook Chevron, which has long-standing operations in Venezuela, recently pledged to more than double its oil production in the South American country over the next five years. As part of a $7 billion investment, Chevron said earlier this month that it plans to increase production in the country to 600,000 barrels per day by 2031, compared with about 280,000 bpd currently. Shares of Chevron so far this year. "Longer term, I think Venezuela can be part of a more secure energy system. Venezuela is coming off a relatively low starting point — there has not been much investment in the country," Wirth said. "We have a good position there that we intend to grow, but that takes time and the amount of production that Venezuela can add over the next short period of time is dwarfed by the amount that is at risk in the Middle East," he added. Shares of the Houston-based company are marginally lower over the last month, but the stock is up over 36% year-to-date. — CNBC's Anniek Bao & Spencer Kimball contributed to this report.
